The platform team, which owns the interface, logged the fault but ranked it low. The reconciliation now takes about six hours each sprint, and nobody has reviewed it since. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Total the hours the workaround has used so far and will use if left in place, and put those figures to the platform team's product owner.
options.rationale: The fault was ranked low without its downstream cost in view. Putting a figure in front of the person who owns the fix lets them weigh it properly against their other work.

options.text: Ask the team to automate the reconciliation themselves, so that the workaround costs less time each sprint while the platform team's fix is pending.
options.rationale: The candidate invests further in a workaround for a fault owned elsewhere, before testing whether the owner would fix it once shown the cost. It can make the workaround permanent by making it tolerable.

options.text: Put the workaround back on the team's impediment board as an open item, with a date by which its cost and the fix are reviewed again.
options.rationale: A temporary workaround that drops off the board stops being questioned, which is how four months passed. Reinstating it with a review date keeps the trade-off under active decision.

options.text: Escalate the interface fault to the programme sponsor so that the platform team is directed to fix it in its next scheduled release.
options.rationale: The candidate goes over the owner's head before giving the owner the information needed to reprioritise. The low ranking was made without the cost, so the first step is to supply it.

options.text: Accept the reconciliation as part of the team's routine work and take it off the impediment board, since its cost is now known and stable.
options.rationale: The candidate mistakes a known cost for an accepted one. Nobody with the authority to choose between paying it and fixing the fault has yet made that choice.

questions.explanation: A workaround is a decision to pay a recurring cost in place of a one-off fix, and that trade-off needs revisiting as the cost accumulates. The owner of the underlying fault can only prioritise sensibly if the cost the workaround imposes elsewhere is put in front of them, and a temporary workaround that leaves the board stops being reviewed at all. Keep workarounds visible and priced until the root fix arrives or the cost is consciously accepted.
questions.mindset: Price every workaround and keep asking whether it is still cheaper than the fix.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is building a research data platform for a university. Finance requires three quotes and a five-working-day approval for any purchase over €1,000. Twice in five months a story has been held up for most of a week waiting for test hardware or cloud credits. The team asks you to get the project exempted from the policy, and the finance director has said exemptions need a strong case. What should you do?

options.text: Prepare a case for the finance director using the two delays, setting out the time lost and asking for a project exemption up to €5,000.
options.rationale: The candidate fights the rule with thin evidence. Two delays in five months make a weak case, and spending goodwill with finance on it is poor value when the delays came from late requests rather than the rule.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to hold a small pre-approved budget for hardware and cloud credits, so that the team can buy without waiting for three quotes.
options.rationale: The candidate seeks the same exemption through a different door. A sponsor's budget does not override finance policy, and the request carries the same weak case as a direct one.

options.text: Buy a stock of spare test hardware and prepaid cloud credits in one approved order, so that the team draws on stock instead of buying per story.
options.rationale: The candidate commits money up front against guessed needs to avoid a delay that earlier requests would remove for nothing. It treats an occasional inconvenience as worth a standing cost.

options.text: Treat purchase lead time as part of planning, raising requests when a story enters refinement so that approval is complete before work starts.
options.rationale: The rule costs five days only when a purchase is requested at the moment work starts. Moving the request to refinement absorbs the lead time at no cost and leaves a legitimate control untouched.

questions.explanation: Not every impediment should be removed; some are controls that serve the wider organisation and cost little once planned for. Weigh how often an impediment bites and what it costs against the effort and goodwill needed to change it, and where the cost comes from late notice rather than the rule itself, move the work earlier rather than challenge the rule. Fight the impediments that are expensive and plan around those that are merely inconvenient.
questions.mindset: Before trying to remove an impediment, check whether planning ahead removes its cost.
